title: Geometric representation of the fractional knapsack problem
summary: Represent item weight by rectangle width, value per unit weight by height, and item value by area to show which items to take first when capacity is limited.
context: Fractional knapsack allows splitting an item and taking only part of it, earning value proportional to the weight taken. Knapsack capacity is 50; because value = weight × value per unit weight, plotting item weight as rectangle width and value per unit weight as height makes rectangle area equal item value.
description: Five adjacent rectangles are ordered from left to right by decreasing height; the fruit icons' names, original IDs, widths, and heights appear in the table below. Beneath the horizontal axis, a double-headed arrow marks knapsack capacity 50, spanning the full width of the leftmost banana rectangle and extending partway into the second rectangle (pineapple).

The diagram directly labels rectangle widths, heights, and capacity 50. Full-item values, weights taken, and values taken in the table below are computed from those labels. The item IDs come from the earlier item table; the total value 277.5 is not printed separately in this figure.

frames.title: Capacity 50 captures the area of the two highest-unit-value segments
frames.explanation: Banana first uses 20 of the capacity 50, leaving 30 to take three-quarters of the pineapple's width 40 while leaving weight 10 behind; the remaining three rectangles lie outside the capacity span. The captured area totals 20 × 6 + 30 × 5.25 = 277.5, giving the maximum total value.
